A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same temporal-leakage study. All nine pages of each version, including figures, tables and appendices, support comparison. The retained Google experiments can be matched across the reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports an original Google audit covering 393 questions and 38,879 URLs, forecasting results on 93 questions, and human validation of 134 documents.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds a DuckDuckGo audit covering 389 questions and 34,454 URLs, including leakage prevalence and temporal breakdowns.

M1.justification: The leakage rubric, MMR processing, judge model, judge prompt and forecasting prompt remain unchanged. The resolved answer newly listed in Section 3.2 was already included in v1 Appendix D.2. Prompt-development explanations disclose existing methodology rather than establish a changed procedure.

E1.justification: The audit expands from Google alone to a second retrieval environment, DuckDuckGo, with 34,454 retrieved URLs. This substantially broadens the search environments tested while retaining the Metaculus forecasting domain and underlying question collection.

E2.justification: DuckDuckGo's date-range retrieval is newly evaluated alongside Google's before: retrieval in the leakage-prevalence and temporal comparisons. The five forecasting comparison conditions in Table 2 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The added DuckDuckGo experiment uses a date range starting on 2000-01-01 and ending at each question's opening date, with usable results for 389 of 393 questions. The Google and 93-question forecasting protocols remain unchanged. Expanded annotation descriptions do not establish a protocol revision.

E4.justification: Section 4.4 extends the cutoff-year analysis to DuckDuckGo, testing whether the temporal pattern appears across engines. The document-level severity breakdown in v1 Appendix B disappears. The four leakage-mechanism case studies remain, and several other appendix statistics survive in tables.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The human-validation sample remains 134 documents, with unchanged headline agreement measures; no new uncertainty-estimation practice is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial DuckDuckGo results: 81.2% of questions have major leakage, 54.8% have direct-answer leakage, and 34.5% of URLs contain post-cutoff information, plus yearly breakdowns. Google forecasting values remain unchanged, including Brier scores 0.242 and 0.108. v1's explicit per-class judge metrics and document-severity counts are removed, although the confusion matrix remains.

T1.justification: The leakage definition and 0–4 scoring rubric are unchanged. Neither version introduces formal theorems or proofs, and no mathematical assumptions or derivations are added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion explicitly frame unreliability across Google and DuckDuckGo and qualify the insufficiency claim as applying to these engines. The central diagnosis, forecasting-inflation claim, claimed systematic-audit novelty and recommendation for frozen snapshots remain.

C2.justification: v2 expands the single-model limitation into a specific concern about shared interpretation errors between judge and forecaster. It also explicitly acknowledges that proposed mitigations were not experimentally evaluated. The leakage mechanisms, corroboration explanation and older-cutoff interpretation remain substantively unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a repository link announcing release of questions, generated queries, retrieved URLs and the audit period. Sections 3.2–3.3 newly explain iterative prompt development using the human-annotated set, disjoint initial annotation, cross-review and consensus resolution. These substantially expand reproducibility information; repository availability was not externally checked.

R1.justification: v2 adds Schlichtkrull et al. on claim verification, Zou et al. on Autocast, and Zheng et al. on LLM judging, while removing Schoenegger et al. It adds a limitation of historical forecasting corpora for modern models. Other preprint-to-publication updates retain the same cited works.

P1.justification: The title and selected passages in the abstract, introduction, methodology, conclusion and limitations are revised. Appendix subsections are reordered and renamed, and the LLM-use statement becomes Acknowledgments. The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The displays are substantially reorganized: Table 1 becomes an engine comparison, v1's temporal Figure 2 becomes v2 Table 3, appendix distribution plots and the detailed classification table disappear, and the example-question table becomes prose. The retained confusion matrix is rendered more clearly and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The DuckDuckGo audit addresses v1's single-engine limitation, while clearer annotation disclosures, a link to audit materials and more specific limitations improve transparency. These benefits outweigh the removal of detailed appendix summaries, but forecasting evidence remains Google-only and relies on the same model for judging and forecasting. The net quality improvement is limited.
